title: Interactive Photoelectric Effect: Photon Energy, Work Function, and Electron Emission
pedagogical_goal: Explore how photon frequency and intensity affect electron emission from a metal surface, visualize Einstein's photoelectric equation (K_max = hν - φ), and understand the threshold frequency concept through interactive sliders and real-time kinetic energy calculations.

fundamental_laws: Einstein's Photoelectric Equation: K_max = hν - φ, where K_max is maximum kinetic energy of emitted electrons, h is Planck's constant, ν is photon frequency, and φ is work function of the metal
Photon Energy: E_photon = hν = hc/λ, where c is speed of light and λ is wavelength
Threshold Condition: Photoelectric emission occurs only when ν ≥ ν₀ (threshold frequency) or equivalently λ ≤ λ₀ (threshold wavelength)
Electron Current Proportionality: Number of photoelectrons per second (and thus photocurrent) is proportional to light intensity for ν > ν₀

components.description: Layer 1: Structural background grid pattern with subtle hexagonal lattice (representing metal crystal structure) and technical boundary benchmarks (width: 960, height: 480). Includes faint coordinate axes and measurement markings.

Layer 2: Massive closed outer structural silhouette of a vacuum phototube occupying >= 65% of viewport area. Features a cylindrical glass envelope with metal cathode (photoemissive surface) on left and anode on right, connected to external circuit. Path uses multi-point Bezier coordinates for realistic tube shape.

Layer 3: Volumetric filled medium representing photon flux (left to right) and electron cloud near cathode. Uses linear gradient for photon beam intensity that changes opacity and color based on intensity variable, and radial gradient for electron emission zone that expands with photoelectron rate. Includes glow filter that pulses with emission events.

<radialGradient id="electronGradient" cx="50%" cy="50%" r="50%"> <stop offset="0%" stop-color="#f43f5e" stop-opacity="0.8"/> <stop offset="100%" stop-color="#f43f5e" stop-opacity="0.0"/> </radialGradient>

components.description: Layer 4: 30 animated entities - 15 photon particles (blue spheres) moving left to right at constant speed, and up to 15 photoelectron particles (red spheres) emitted from cathode surface when photon energy exceeds work function. Electrons are accelerated toward anode by electric field, with velocity proportional to sqrt(max_kinetic_energy).

Layer 5: In-situ labels and dynamic readouts directly on the visual stage: (1) Photon energy badge near photon beam, (2) Work function annotation on cathode surface, (3) Stopping potential meter between electrodes, (4) Kinetic energy display near anode, (5) Threshold wavelength marker on spectrum scale.

Use gsap.context() inside useEffect for flawless cleanup on re-render
MANDATE REAL KINETIC TRANSFORMS: Animate translation for photon/electron particles, scale for pulse effects on emission
STRICT PROHIBITION on fake animations that merely toggle strokeDasharray on static lines

pedagogical_callouts.title: Photon Absorption
pedagogical_callouts.text: Incoming photons strike the metal surface. Only photons with energy exceeding the work function (E_photon > φ) can eject electrons.

pedagogical_callouts.title: Electron Emission & Kinetic Energy
pedagogical_callouts.text: Ejected electrons gain kinetic energy equal to the excess photon energy: K.E. = hν - φ. This kinetic energy determines their speed toward the anode.

pedagogical_callouts.title: Intensity vs. Frequency Effects
pedagogical_callouts.text: Increasing light intensity increases the NUMBER of emitted electrons (brightness of beam) but does NOT change their kinetic energy. Increasing frequency (decreasing wavelength) increases the ENERGY of each emitted electron.

pedagogical_callouts.title: Threshold Frequency Concept
pedagogical_callouts.text: Below a critical threshold frequency (or above threshold wavelength), no electrons are emitted regardless of light intensity. This demonstrates the particle nature of light and contradicts classical wave theory predictions.
